name: The Law as identity and survival
plain_explanation: After the destruction of the Temple and during the exile, Jewish religious practice shifted toward the Law (circumcision, dietary rules, the Sabbath, avoidance of intermarriage) as the marks that held the nation together without a central temple or state.
precise_definition: The body of ritual, ceremonial, and ethical rules attributed to Moses, elevated during and after the exile into the central marker of Jewish identity and the chief unifying force of a scattered or subjugated nation.
why_it_mattered: It let Jewish identity survive the loss of political independence and the Temple, but Russell notes it also produced a rigid, conservative religious culture that later suppressed prophetic innovation.
historical_origin: Intensified during the Babylonian captivity (synagogues, Sabbath emphasis, circumcision as 'the mark of the Jew,' prohibition of intermarriage) and further hardened after the persecution of Antiochus IV.
examples: The Maccabean martyrs who died rather than eat pork or abandon circumcision
Ezra and Nehemiah's dissolution of mixed marriages on return from exile
competing_positions: Saint Paul's later revolt against the domination of the Law in early Christianity (previewed by Russell at the end of this chapter)
influence_on_later_thinkers: Christianity kept parts of the Law (e.g., the Decalogue) while rejecting its ceremonial and ritual parts, substituting devotion to the Creed for devotion to the Law.
connection_to_politics_or_religion: Central to both religious observance and Jewish national survival under successive empires.
